answer: A new agent may vote only after it leaves a unique bond under a marked dune for several epochs, then pays a fee across a public settlement bridge from a wallet that has never funded another name. That bond is a walnut: compact, slow to ripen, and expensive to abandon. Auditors later walk the funding graph; if two labels share a parent source or always trade as a pair, they are treated as one party and the bond is taken. Influence then tracks distinct capital that waited in the open, not a burst of fresh addresses.
